HOMAGE TO SHAHEED-E-WATAN, ASHFAQULLAH KHAN 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon'ble Members, today is the Martyrdom Day of 
Shaheed-e-Watan, Ashfaqullah Khan, a great martyr of "Kokori Rail Dacoity 
Case." Ashfaqullah Khan belonged to the stream of nationalism which 
glorified India's stuggle for freedom with the blood of martyrs. He was the 
forerunner, who inspired Bhagat Singh and others in their revolutionary 
activities. Ashfaqullah Khan participated in the Kakori Rail Dacoity, 
alongwith Pandit Rama Prasad Bismil and eight others. He also participated 
in the raids by the revolutionaries at Sherganj, Bichpuri and Mainpuri, and at 
other places. 
Ashfaqullah Khan, alongwith Rama Prasad, Roshan Singh and Rajendra 
Lahiri, was sentenced to death in the Kakori Rail Dacoity case. The Kakori 
case trial brought the entire nation together to defend Ashfaqullah and his 
revolutionary comanions. The British Government did not yield to any 
appeals made by the leaders. Ashfaqullah, Rama Prasad Bismil and Roshan 
Singh were executed on the 19th December, 1927. All three greeted death 
bravely with a smile. 
This year also happens to be the birth centenary of Ashfaqullah Khan, and 
in this year and on this martyrdom day, it is important for all of us to recall 
and revive our glorious struggle for freedom. Nation owes a debt of gratitude 
to these revolutionaries for their sacrifice. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence in memory of 
Shaheed-e-Watan, Ashfaqullah Khan. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute}

Setting-up of a National Calamity Contingency Fund 
*422. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the 11th Finance Commission recommended 
the winding-up of the National Fund for Natural Calamity and setting-up of 
a National Calamity Contingency- Fund; 
8 

[19 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have accepted this recommendation and if so, 
when; 
(d) when and in what manner this will be implemented; and 
(c) how the contingency of natural calamity of rare severity will be 
addressed pending the creation of NCCF? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Central Government's role is to supplement the efforts of 
the State Governments for calamity relief. In its recommendations 
concerning calamity relief, the Eleventh Finance Commission has increased 
the size of the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) to Rs. 11007.59 crores, 
compared to Rs. 6304.27 crores under the Tenth Finance Commission, with 
contributions from Centre and States in the ratio of 75:25. EFC has invisaged 
that with the increased transfers under the CRF. States should be able to 
provide immediate relief to the victims of cyclone, drought, floods, 
hailstorm, earthquake and fire. The new NCCF scheme has been provided 
for only calamities of rare nature and extraordinary severe intensity. 
(b) The EFC has recommended creation of National Calamity 
Contingency Fund (NCCF) in the Public Account of the Government of 
India with an initial corpus of Rs. 500 crores as contribution from the 
Government of India. Drawals from the Fund arc to be recouped by the 
imposition of a special surcharge. Assistance from the Fund is to be 
provided for calamity of such a severe nature that would call for financial 
assistance to the affected State over and above what is available in the CRF 
or other Plan/ Non-Plan sources. 
(c) The report of the EFC was laid on the Table of the House on 27th 
July, 2000. The recommendations of Eleventh Finance Commission have 
been accepted by the Government. 
(d) and (e) Guidelines for the ad ministration of the National 
Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) have been issued. The Scheme 
9 

RAJYA SABHA       [19 December, 2000] 
will be deemed to have come into force from 1st April, 2000. The Ministry 
of Finance has moved for the raising of Rs. 500 crores through a 
Supplementary Demand towards the corpus of this Fund in the current 
Session of the Parliament. The Scheme also envisages setting up of National 
Centre for Calamity Management under the Ministry of Agriculture to 
monitor extent of natural calamity and recommend releases of assistance to 
States from the NCCF.

Deregulation of Oil Sector 
*423. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of guidelines worked out for implementing the Kelkar 
Committee recommendations on complete deregulation of the oil sector by 
2002, privatisation of all oil and gas P.S.Us. by 2005 and norms of subsidy 
suggested on L.P.G. and Kerosene to be 15 per cent and 20 per cent, 
respectively, of import parity; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the present subsidy on L.P.G. and Kerosene 
works out to be 25 per cent and 45 per cent of import parity, which is much 
higher than the Kelkar Committee's recommendation; and 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
19 

RAJYA SABHA        [19 December, 2000]  
Statement 
(a) The Government in January 1995, had set up the Kelkar 
Committee to make recommendations on strategic restructuring plan 
of the oil sector. The Committee had inter-alia recommended phased 
reduction in subsidies on domestic LPG and kerosene for public 
distribution and total deregulation of the downstream petroleum 
sector by 31st March, 2002. However, it did not make 
recommendations on norms of subsidy on domestic LPG and 
kerosene for public distribution. Similarly, it did not recommend 
privatisation of all oil and gas PSUs by 2005. 
However, an Expert Technical Group (ETG) was set up by the 
Government in June 1996. The ETG inter-alia recommended a year-by-year 
programme for reduction in subsidies on domestic LPG and kerosene for 
public distribution. After considering the recommendations of ETG, 
Government in November 1997 decided that subsidy level on domestic LPG 
will be reduced to 15% of import parity by 2000-2001; and on kerosene for 
public distribution to 33.33% of the import parity by 2001-2002. On full 
deregulation i.e. effective 1st April 2002, the subsidy on domestic LPG and 
kerosene for public distribution will be transferred to fiscal budget of the 
Government. 
(b) The estimated average subsidy for December 2000, based on 
November 2000 international prices of crude oil and products, is 48% on 
domestic LPG and 53% on kerosene for public distribution. 
(c) Subsidies vary with the changes in the international oil arid product 
prices. Due to high volatility in the international prices of crude oil and 
petroleum products since February 1999, the subsidy level has increased 
inspite of upward revisions in the consumer prices of domestic LPG and 
kerosene for public distribution.

3219. SHRI C. APOK JAMIR: Will the Minister of LAW, 
JUSTICE AND  COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

bankruptcy of State in the event of its failure to discharge its fiscal 
obligations; and

THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITELY): (a) and (c) Th e law relating to insolvency is 
contained in the Presidency- towns Insolvency Act, 1909 (3 of 1909) and the 
Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920 (5 of 1920) in the areas as mentioned therein.

Decongestion of Major Ports 
3264. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
SHIPPING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have chalked out detailed plan to dccongest the 
major Indian ports and make them more functional; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the major ports covered; and 
(c) whether there is any proposal for technological, upgradation of 
some of these ports and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Main reasons for causing 
congestion in the Major Ports are non-availability of adequate berths, 
accumulation of uncleared cargo in the back up area and bunch arrival of 
vessels. Various steps have been taken such as implementation of a number 
of capacity addition schemes, simplification of procedures for disposal of the 
uncleared/unclaimed cargo and regular consultation with the shippers to ensure 
that the vessels are nominated regularly to avoid their bunching. 
(c) The development and modernisation of Major Ports is an ongoing 
continuous process. The development programmes being undertaken at present lay 
emphasis on enhancing standards of Major Ports and their productivity through 
construction and equipping new berths; acquisition of state-of-the-art equipment 
setting up of Vessel Traffic Management System; labour training and welfare; 
etc.

various watershed development programmes.

 SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: Will the Minister of WATER

(1980) has identified the following rivers which are prone to floods.

Subaranarekha, the Tapti and the Narmada.Coastal areas (deltaic 
Regions) of Mahanadi and Godavari rivers also experience flood.

average annual flow available in these river basins is about 1389.4 Billion 
cubic Metre (BCM) out of which 474.4 BCM is utilizable. The total live

KHANDURI): Madam, I move : 
'That the Bill to give statutory status to the existing Central 
Road Fund governed by the Resolution of Parliament 
passed in 1988, for development and maintenance of 
national highways and improvement of safety at railway 
crossings, and for these purposes to levy and collect by 
way of cess, a duty of excise and duty of customs on 
motor spirit commonly known as petrol, high speed diesel 
oil and other matters connected therewith, as passed by the 
Lok Sabha, be taken Into consideration." 
Before 1 make a request to pass the* Bill, with your 
permission, 1 would Hke to say a few words. Madam, in our country, 
there Is a vast network of roads, stre tching to over 3.3 million km, that 
Is, about 33 iakh km of roads. Out of this, there are 57, 737 Kms of 
National Highways. The development of roads In this big country has 
not realty kept pace, the way, it should have, basically because of 
paucity of funds. And therefore, a long term strategy, a sustained 
Ananda! arrangement.had to be made, and for development of roads, 
this sort of exercise had to be carried out. I may put across to the non. 
Members that such a concept did exist for a long time. The Central 
Road Fund first came 4nto existence in 1920, and thereafter, it 
continued. Some money was collected which was very meagre even 
for roads. But it was in 1077 that the Parliament passed a Resolution 
and decided that not less than 3.5 paisa per litre of petrol should be 
levied for the purposes of development of roads In this country. This 
went on, and at this rate, we collected about Rs. 25 to 30 crores per 
year, which was being distributed in the ratio of 80:20 to the States 
and the Centre. Subsequently, In May 1988, another Resolution was 
passed by the Parliament, according to which not less than 5 per cent 
of the cost of petrol and diesel was to be levied for the purposes of this 
Fund. This cess was to be distributed In the ratio of 64 per cent to the 
States, 35.5 per cent to the Centre and half a per cent for the 
administration of this Fund. However, this Resolution was never 
implemented from 1988 toi998. This remained unimplemented 
because it was all the time under examination, and for some reason or 
the other,  it could  not  be Implemented.     Thereafter, in  1998,  a 
cess was 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2000] 
introduced for petrol at the rate of one rupee per litre. This was during the financial 
year 1008-99, and it was effective from 2nd June, 1998. In the subsequent year, 
1999-2000, a cess on diesel was also introduced at the same scale, that Is, one 
rupee per litre, and it became effective from 1st March, 1999. The allocation norms 
for this Fund were also decided, and according to them, out of the diesel 
collection, 50 per cent, that is, 50 paisa would go straight to the rural roads 
through the States. The balance 50 per cent, plus the cess on petrol would again be 
combined, and of this, 57.5 per cent would be given to the Centre, 30 per cent to 
the States, 12-1/2 per cent to the Railways for the purposes of providing safety at the 
level crossings, constructing railway over-bridges etc., and thus, it was distributed to 
the States as well as to the Centre. Out of the 30 per cent to be given to the 
States, 3 per cent was kept aside by the Centre for the purposes of developing 
within the States inter-State roads or places of economic importance, and thus, 
this cess was introduced and the distribution was made. Now, a question has 
come up here, and there was also an observation about the Ordinance. I would 
tike to explain this thing to the House. Although I agree in principle that an Ordinance 
should not be Issued when the Parliament is about to meet, but in this case, I 
would like to Inform the House that it was done in good faith and with good 
intention. The reason was that this money was available but we had no legal 
instrument to distribute it In the way I have just mentioned. Therefore, this decision 
was taken. This money was available. The States were saying that soon after the 
monsoon, they will be demanding the money. The working season was available 
after October- November, and therefore, if we had to wait, in that event, we would 
have lost two months, the month of November and December, because it was 
required to be passed here, then the normal procedure was to be followed, and 
probably, by January, we would have been able to allot the money. I would like 
to inform the House that because of the Ordinance, Rs. 990 crores have been 
sub-allotted to the States, out of which, one-third has already been distributed. 
Therefore, the aim of this Ordinance was that we make money available to the 
States. Many State Chief Ministers have written letters requesting that money be 
made available. .There was a working season, and that is why, the first Instalment 
has been sent, and therefore, I inform the House that this Ordinance has been 
issued with good Intention. The salient features of this Bill are four. Firstly, it gives 
statutory status to the Central Road Fund and to the Resolution of 1988. Secondly, 
this Fund will go straight to the Consolidated Fund, and thereafter, the 
Parliament will enable It to be

SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA {W est Bengal): Madam Deputy 
Chairman, I wonder why this kind of an important Bill was not brought 
by the Government much earlier, when it was expected much earlier, 
and when there was a national consensus, in order to ensure a 
smooth development of the nation and in order to have a modern 
transport system. The Central Road Fund Ordinance was brought 
before both Houses of Parliament 12 years back, but I wonder why 
Government after Government never considered to replace the 
Ordinance with a Bill of the kind that has come now. Anyway, I thank 
the present Minister for having brought this Bill. The only thing is that it 
should have been brought much earlier because there was no dispute 
over this; there was a consensus on it, and it was very much 
necessary for the development of the entire nation, in accordance with 
the other development activities that many Central Governments have 
been taking up all these years. 
Now, coming to the specific issue of the Central Road Fund Bill, it 
appears that there has been a certain lack of vision and lack of 
foresightedness on behalf of the Government while planning the entire 
thing. For example, most of the viable ports on the Western Coast of 
our country - these ports are more viable than other ports because 
they are not vulnerable to cyclonic storms and different kinds of 
climatic hazards from which the Visakhapatnam Port and other ports 
on the Eastern coast suffer -- are not connected with any National 
Highway or by? any proposed National Highway or even by the 
proposed Golden Quadrilateral; this  keeps them cut off. The ports of 
Goa, Mangalore and Cochin are the three very Important ports of our 
country.    Not only these; many other small ports still remain cut off

because of lack of foresight and because of the lopsided policy 
perspective of the Government; they remain cut off because none of 
the highways reach up to these ports. So, unless the Government 
mends this situation and takes up the proposed national Golden 
Quadrilateral covering th ese ports, the main objective of having this 
kind of a legislation and the main objective of building National 
Highways all over the country would remain unfulfilled, and It will not 
serve the purpose of development activity that the other Departments 
of the Government or the private sect or is planning for. This will affect 
and hamper the development activity of the country as a whole. This 
will affect our exports. This will affect our Imports. And, the most

large part of time because of lack of proper mode of transport. I want 
the Minister to give adequate attention to this aspect. I cannot mention 
the specifics of it, but I strongly feel that the National Highways, which 
are very much required in certain places, should have been built long 
back, by a firm policy decision of the Government. But these have not 
been built by the Government so far. But, at least, in certain cases,

the North-East, where the States are starved of funds, Is

On behalf of my party and on my own behalf, I support the Central 
Road Fund Bill, 2000. This is an important piece of legislation and it

To develop a country, three things are essential. One is power 
generation; the second is construction of roads; and the third is 
telecommunications. Of course, airports, sea ports and railways are

Works Department, the Department of Rural Development, etc. The 
Ministry of Surface Transport wants to build more National Highways,

imposing cess on petrol and diesel.

6,000 crores. Fifty per cent of the cess from diesel is earmarked for the 
States. The Eleventh Finance Commission is of the view that there is

an arrangement to promote savings and their utilisation for mutual

consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, makes rules under the Act,

demand is so raised from time to time, increase the limits of aggregate

chit amount for individual foreman fr om Rs.25,000/- to Rs. 1,00,000/-

1,00,000/- to Rs.1,00,000/- per partner, subject to a ceiling of 
Rs,6,00,000/-.

amount equal to the chit amount in the name of the Registrar in an

THE JUVENILE JUSTICE (CARE AND PROTECTION OF 
CHILDREN) BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI) : 
Madam, I move: 
"That the Bill to consolidate and amend the law relating to 
juveniles in conflict with law an d children in need of care and 
protection by providing for proper care, protection and 
treatment by catering to their development needs, and by 
adopting a child-friendly approach 
292 

[ 19 December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
in the adjudication and disposition of matters in the best 
interest of children and for thei r ultimate rehabilitation through 
various institutions established under this enactment, as 
passed by Lok Sabha,   be taken into consideration," 
Madam, the Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 enacted by Parliament 
to provide for care, protection, development and rehabilitation of 
neglected or delinquent juveniles has been in force since 2nd October, 
1887. The Government felt that provisions of the Act were not 
addressing the issues of care and protection of neglected children 
adequately. 
The revision of the current Act has been pending for sometime 
and a review of the Act and its implementation over the years revealed 
a number of deficiencies/shortcomings warranting extensive 
amendments in the Act. The Bill which is now before this august 
House for consideration is an attempt to make the judicial system 
more child friendly and accessible to a juvenile/child or anyone on 
their behalf, including the police, voluntary organisations, social 
workers or parents and guardians throughout the country,  and provide 
for rehabilitation of the destitute child. 
The present Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 Is not in conformity 
with International Conventions on the Rights of the Child, ratified by 
India, such as the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the 
United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Administration of 
Juvenile Justice, 1995. These Conventions have prescribed a set of 
standards to be adhered to by all State parties in securing the best 
interests of the child. CRC being a subsequent development to the 
enactment of Juvenile Justice Act, 1986, it was essential that the 
Juvenile Justice Act is amended to bring it In conformity with CRC. 
The Government has consulted expert and knowledgeable 
people in the field, because Justice Ranganath Mishra had raised this 
issue and said that there was a problem. I just want to tell htm the kind 
of people that we have consulted. It has taken me two years to bring 
this Bill which, according to me, was the best, possible I could do. We 
have consulted Justice Krishna Iyer, Justice Bhattacharjee, Justice 
Jeevan Reddy, Chairman, Law Commission of India, Prof. N.R. 
Madhav Menon, Member, Law Commission of India, Dr K.N. 
Chandrasekharan Pillai, School of Legal Studies, Cochin, Dr. B. B. 
Pandey, University of Delhi, Ms Vibha Parthasarthy,  Chairperson,  
National Commission  for Women,  Ms Sheela 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2000] 
Barse, NEERGAURAV, Mumbai; Ms Indira Jaisingh, Senior Advocate, 
New Delhi. Ms Aparna Bhatt, Human Rights Law Network, Delhi, Prof. 
B.N. Chattoraj, National Institute of Criminology and Forensic Science, 
New Delhi, Shri Rajeev Dhawan, Senior Advocate, New Delhi, Ms Meera 
C. Saksena, Secretary to the Government of Karnataka, Women and 
Child Development Department, Bangalore. We have then gone to Dr. 
Hira Singh, former Director, NISD. New Delhi, consulted NGOs like 
Ms Rita Panicker, Butterflies, New Delhi; Mr. Ossie Femandes, Human 
Rights Advocacy and Research Foundation, Chennai. This shows that we 
have consulted many experts and knowledgeable people. 
Finally, the Bill was drafted by the Law School, Bangalore. After 
they have drafted it, we held a series of consultations with Judges and 
other legal luminaries, including heads of police, the Councils for Child 
Welfare, officials of the Planning Commission, officials of the Law 
Ministry, the Director of Child Line Organisation which is doing an 
excellent work for the street children and other people. So, this is 
possibly the best we could do. I don't think they have made mistakes 
with the spirit and text of the Bill. 
If I am deviating from this. I could have said it at the end. But I 
would like to say regarding the adoption of children in need of care and 
protection or orphaned, abandoned, missing, abused children, including 
children whose families are in crisis and several other exploited children; 
these categories of children have a right to a family. This Bill provides 
for the rehabilitation of such children. Adoption has been provided as 
one of the met hods for rehabilitation of the orphaned, abandoned, 
neglected and exploited children. This has been provided for such 
categories of children who have no identity of their own, irrespective of 
caste, creed or religion. After adoption, the children wilI get an identity 
of their adopted parents. This provision is based on article 21 of the 
United Nations Convention on the Rights of Child; and specific powers 
have been assigned to competent authorities to give children on 
adoption, and various procedures are involved for the same. This 
measure in no way undermines the personal law of a community and 
the proposed adopted parents can always adopt such children,  as per 
the personal law concerning their religion. 
To come back to it, the review of the present Act by such 
experts has revealed that a large number of amendments would have 
to be made in 
294 

[ 19 December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the Act. Therefore, it was decided to bring forth a fresh Bill    before 
this august House replacing the present   Juvenile Justice Act, 1986. 
I would like to highlight the salient features of the proposed 
Bill which are as follows: - 
(1) It would separate the Act into two parts - one for juveniles in 
conflict with law; and the other for the juvenile/children in 
need of care and protection which will give the clarity and 
distinction in the treatment. 
(2) The    proposed    Bill    will    make    the    justice    system    
for juvenile/children more appreciative of the developmental 
needs in comparison to criminal justice system as applicable 
to adults. At the moment, we treat all children, those who 
are abandoned and destitutes,  as potential criminals. 
(3) It brings the juvenile law in conformity with the CRC. It 
prescribes a uniform age of eighteen years for both boys 
and girls,   as per article 1 of CRC 
It ensures speedy disposal of cases within a limited period of 
four months. It spells out the role of the State as a facilitator rather 
than a doer by involving voluntary organisations and local bodies in 
the implementation of this Act. It proposes creating special juvenile 
police units. This is for the first time that we have suggested this in 
India that we have child-friendly police units, with a humane approach 
through sensitisation and training. It would enable increased 
accessibility to juveniles by establishing the Juvenile Justice Board 
and the Child Welfare Committees and Homes in each district or 
group of districts. It contains effective provisions for various 
alternatives for rehabilitation and so cial reintegration, such as 
adoption, foster care, sponsorship and aftercare of abandoned, 
destitute, neglected and delinquent juveniles, as provided in articles 
18 to 21 of the CRC. I hope that with the enactment of the Bill, the 
children in need of care and protection, would get a better deal. At 
least, they will get coverage by law which they do not have, at the 
moment. With the creation of ad equate infrastructure for the 
implementation of the Act, with the involvement of informal systems, 
especially the family, voluntary organisations and the community, our 
objective to treat the children in the best possible manner

society, will be achieved. Thank you.

3319. DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the incorrect decision by the Director General, 
Naval Project, Mumbai to allow the refund to the contractor for excess 
consumption of cement led to extra expenditure of about Rs. 64 crores;

(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that the Navy has used a life expired sonar 
cable causing loss of sonar dome; and 
(e) if so, what steps have been taken so as to.stop recurrence of such 
instance in future? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERN ANDES): (a) to 
(e) The Director General Naval Project, Mumbai, had concluded a contract for 
pre-casting of 52,000 cubic meter of concrete cement blocks for a Naval project. 
The contract specified the technical sp ecification for the concrete mix for 
ensuring the required strength and workability characteristic. It also specified the 
minimum quantity (400 Kg) of cement to be used in each cubic meter of 
concrete mix. However additional cement beyond the specified minimum 
quantity, was used by the contractor to achieve the desired quality. The actual 
quantity of cement used was between 410 Kg and 460 Kg for each cubic 
meter of concrete mix as against the minimum quantity of 400 Kg specified in 
the contract. In the period January, 1996 to July, 1998, DGNP was effecting 
deductions from the contractor for the cost of additional quantity of the 
departmentally supplied cement from the payments due to contractor. The 
contractor had represented against such deductions on the ground that use of 
additional cement was an-essential technical requirement of the department, 
based on the laboratory test, for which he was not liable, as his original 
quotation for the work was based on the minimum quantity specified in the 
tender document. 
65 

RAJYA SABHA       [20 December, 2000]

Projects, Mumbai and was considered to be valid. As such, DGNP agreed to 
refund Rs. 63.81 lakhs for deductions made. 
Audit have commented on the decision of Director General, Naval Project, 
Mumbai to refund the cost of excess consumption cement to the contractor. The 
observation of audit in the matter is being examined. 
The electronics end of the Towed Sonar was lost from an Indian Naval Ship in 
September, 1998 due to localized corrosion at the joints of the towing cables and 
not due to use of life expired cable. Necessary corrective actions have been 
implemented to prevent occurrence of  corrosion by improved protective 
material.

3380. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "India's power reforms are a non-starter" published in the 'Business 
Standard* dated the 17th September, 2000; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) the steps takeivfcroposed to be taken regarding the problems7 raised in the 
said news-item; and 
(d) what steps have been taken or proposed to be taken to make India an 
alternative destination for investment in power sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (d) Financial closure of a number of 
Independent Power Projects (IPPs) is held up due to non-availability of 
escrowable capacity with the SEBs to provide payment security to these 
projects. The various steps taken by Government regarding the problems raised 
in the said news-item and to make India an attractive destination for investment in 
power sector include the following:— 
(i) The issue of reforms of SEBs wa s discussed in the Power Ministers 
Conference held in February, 2000. It was resolved that reforms must be 
undertaken with determination, vigour and a sense of urgency. The key 
elements of the reforms strategy are:—  
(a) Energy Audit at all levels. 
121 

RAJYA SABHA       [20 December. 2000] 
(b) Time bound programme of 100% metering of all consumers by 
December, 2001. 
(c) Reduction and finally, elemination of power theft within a specified 
time frame.

distribution system by taking sub-station as a unit on a 
priority basis. 
If   the   above   appears   unattainable   in   the  existing  set   up, 
corporatization/cooperatization/privatization   of   distribution,   would 
have to be undertaken. 
(ii) Based on discussions with the Financial Institutions, it has been 
agreed that financing of IPPs would be linked with achievement of 
reforms linked milestones by the States. 
(iii) Raising the limit of power projects which do not require the 
clearance from CEA. 
(iv) Minimizing the role of Foreign Investment Promotion Board by 
providing for automatic approval for foreign equity in selected 
categories and enlarging the provisions for automatic approval for 
such projects. Accordingly, projects for electric generation, 
transmission and distribution will be permitted foreign equity 
participation upto 100% on the automatic approval route without any 
limit.

the pace of hydro power development in order to exploit the vast 
hydro-electric potential at a faster pace, increase private 
investment and promote small and mini hydel projects. 
(vii) The development of mega power projects at mine pit* heads,

(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) No targets for rural electrification

(b) Rural Electrification is the responsibility of the State Electricity

last few years. The major reasons for slow progress are financial constraints

3385.   DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD: 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to review the performance of the 
National thermal power stations with a view to renovate and modernise them 
for increasing efficiency of the plants; 
(b) if so, the action taken in this regard; and 
(c) whether the latest technology of super critical boilers is likely to be 
inducted? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) The Government have 
reviewed the performance of old thermal stations in order to improve their 
efficiency by carrying out Renovation and Modernisation (R&M) and Life 
Extension (L.E.) works. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) have 
formulated a National Perspective Plan upto the year 2011-12 for R&M and 
L.E. of thermal power stations in the country. NTPC has already initiated R&M 
process of some of their old thermal plants like Talcher and Tanda TPS, 
Singrauli, Korba, Ramagundam and Vindhyachal STPS. 
(c) NTPC has planned to adopt super critical technology for its new 
coal based power plants comprising 660 MW units for achieving higher plant 
efficiency. This will help in reducing fuel consumption, particulate emission 
and green house gases. NTPC has  already   received  Techno-Economic  
Clearance   (TEC)   from 
132 

[20 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
Central Electricity Authority (CEA ) for its Sipat Stage-I (3x660 MW) 
project based on super critical technology. 
Standardisation of Electrical Equipments 
33S6. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether   Government   propose   to   standardize   electrical 
equipments; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the present status? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI   JAYAWANTI   MEHTA):    (a)   and   (b)   Energy 
Management Centre (EMC) was established in the year 1989 under the 
Society Registration Act. In order to provide a legal framework for 
undertaking energy conservation measures, the Energy Conservation Bill 
2000 was introduced. The Bill was referred to the Standing Committee of 
Parliament on Energy on 25.2.2000. The Standing Committee has submitted 
their report to the Speaker of Lok Sabha on 6th November 2000 
recommending enactment of the Bill with certain modifications. The revised 
EC Bill incorporating the recommendations made by the Standing 
Committee will be introduced in the Parliament during the Budget Session. 
The Bill, inter alia, would enable Government to fix minimum energy 
efficiency standards for the notified equipments and appliances which 
consume, generate, transmit or suppl y energy. Electrical equipments and 
appliances of common use like a geyser, air conditioner, iron box, 
refrigerators etc., which are energy intensive will be notified for fixing energy 
consumption standards in the initial years. While fixing energy consumption 
standards in respect of these equipments and appliances; the technology 
available and cost involved in upgradation would be kept in view.

Statement 
Major   findings   of   Concurrent   Evaluation   of   Intergrated   Rural 
Development Programme (IRDP) conducted during 1995-96 
1. Almost 85% of the old beneficiaries crossed the earlier poverty line 
of Rs. 6400/- and a little over 46% crossed the revised poverty line 
of Rs.  11000/-. 
2. More or less similar results for SC & ST beneficiaries crossing the 
poverty line. 
3. A little over 75% of the old beneficiaries and 93% new 
beneficiaries did not report any sale of IRDP assets. 
4. The average net income of old beneficiaries was Rs. 2498/ for the 
primary, secondary and tertiary sector put together. 
5. The quality of productive assets was reported to be good in the case 
of a little over 94% of old beneficiaries and 87% new beneficiaries. 
6. 71 to 78% beneficiaries reported  the assistance for purchase of 
assets as adequate. 
202 

[20 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
7. A little over 14% women headed households r eceived IRDP 
assistance. In about 51% villages economic activities were 
disrupted due to natural calamities. 
8. Gram Sabha selected only about 26%  beneficiaries. 
9. Officials selected 56% beneficiaries. 
 
10. Only 48% of the assets were insured. 
11. Time taken for sanction of loan was a month only in 24% cases. 
12. 45% beneficiaries reported 2 or more weeks wage loss for follow 
up of the cases. 
13. 42% of the beneficiaries reported assets to be not in use. 
14. 55% reported over dues, out of which 23% reported to be willful 
defaulters. 
15. 22% reported making payment by way of consideration to the 
Government/Bank staff for getting IRDP assistance. 
Major findings of the impact assessment studies conducted in 1999 are 
given below: 
1. Majority of the recipents of assistance for creating assets was 
earning viable income from the scheme. 
2. Increment in employment days and income has resulted in better 
quality of meal. 
3. Shortage of personnel and resources is a major hurdle in 
implementation of programmes. 
4. The target group enjoys better standard of living in the villages 
which indicates that impact of  these programmes has been 
favourable in the past in raising the standard of living of the poor 
people. 
5. Transparency in selection of benefi ciaries, maintenance of records, 
and maintenance of databases needs improvement. 
6. Despite many problems, the poverty alleviation programmes had 
definitely made an impact. All stakeholders had reported 
203 

RAJYA SABHA       [28 December, 2W8] 
that although piecemeal, the villages had certainly progressed in the past 
three years, especially due to the creation of community assets like 
roads, water points, essential buildings like the school, etc. There were 
reports of increasing affordabality for basic necessities and other 
household expenses. In many cases, the additional income had been 
diverted to the education of the children. Beneficiaries from the MWS 
had reported increasing productivity of crops and a rise in agricultural 
income. 
7. Under N©APS most of the beneficiaries received benefits in time. 43 
per cent of the beneficiaries were women. 40 per cent of the 
beneficiaries under the scheme said that the pension is not paid 
regularly. 
8. There is a need to have profes sional and realistic approach for 
identification of viable projects, be it for the beneficiaries or for the 
village. 
9. Beneficiaries specially under IRDP and DWCRA find it very difficult to 
market the products manufactured by them. This is due to lack of quality 
of the product being manufactured. There is need to adopt appropriate 
technology to suit rural entrepreneurs and create awareness among the 
beneficiaries regarding the importance of maintaining quality. 
10. Most of the projects identified under the various programmes suffer mainly 
due to unscientific way of fixing the project cost.

Discouraging export of Raw Cotton 
† 3455. SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
    SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to  a study, an income of Rs. 100 
crores which is being earned by selling a certain quantum of cotton at present 
can be increased to the tune of Rs. 800 crores by selling the cloth prepared 
by the same quantum of cotton; 
(b) if not, what is Government's assessment in this regard; 
(c) whether Government propose to formulate any incentive scheme to 
discourage the export of  raw material in the textile industry and instead 
promote the export of finished products; and 
(d) if so, the broad outlines thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAYA KUMAR): (a) and (b) The value addition imparted to 
raw cotton is generally in the range of four to twel'e times depending upon 
the nature and type of textile products. 
(c) and (d) Export of raw cotton is allowed taking into account the 
availability of raw cotton and demand of domestic industry. Government 
have taken various initiatives for promotion of exports of finished textile 
products which include the implementation of Technology Up gradation Fund 
Schemes (TUFS), Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC) mainly for 
strengthening of overall viability and sharpening the competitive edge of the 
textile industry in the domestic and international markets, and adoption of 
the new National Textile Policy-2000 with objectives, inter alia, to facilitate 
the textile industry to attain and sustain a pre-eminent global standing in the 
manufacture and export of. clothing and other finished textile products.

by the hon. Railway Minister that she had given up the right to issue

issuing free railway passes continues, and she is also exercising her

were tabled in the House, immediately, in the afternoon, the Railway 
Ministry, without informing anybody, and that too outside the House,

correction on the statement which was laid on the Table of the House

SPECIAL MENTIONS  
Appropriate and timely action against banned Organisations 
SHRI ONWARD L. NONGTDU (Meghalaya): Sir, the banning of two 
253 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2000] 
militant organisations, namely, the Hynviewtrep National Liberation 
Council and the Achick National Volunteer Council, of Meghalaya 
recently has evoked mixed reactions among the masses. 
On the one hand, the people of the State appreciate the steps 
taken by the Central Government to maintain peace and harmony 
and, on the other, the banned outfits have become popular and they 
dare to challenge the Government with dire consequences. 
There is a debate everywhere that in spite of the fact that 
certain organisations were banned in different parts of the country, 
those organisations have become more determined and aggressive, 
and they are causing untold sufferings to the people and a countless 
amount of national loss, both in terms of life and property. 
The Government is bound to take stern necessary follow-up 
measures. The desired results are not achieved because the people's 
cooperation is not forthcoming. This happens because of mental 
corruption. It seems that the whole environment is corrupt, 
economically, politically and otherwise. 
Therefore, banning an organisation calls for an advance, well-
planned and thorough preparedness for taking immediate aggressive 
and appropriate action, before the other side organise themselves for 
a long-drawn battle of survival, prestige and revenge. Otherwise, a 
comparatively peaceful State like Meghalaya would become a battle-
field, where the law-abiding citizens will have to face the nightmare for 
a long time to come. Thank you. 
Pollution of our great rivers of India 
SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA (Karnataka): Sir, we have great 
rivers in our country and they are the main life-line of our activities. 
We get drinking water to feed millions of people from these rivers. Our 
agriculture is also mainly dependant on river water. But our rivers are 
polluted every day by the disposal of dead bodies. The dead bodies 
are thrown into the rivers on religious grounds, thus polluting the 
rivers, which can cause epidemic diseases and play havoc with 
human lives. This unfortunate custom is found all along the course of 
the Ganges and other larger rivers of the country.   This unfortunate 
custom has to be stopped. 
I would like to know the steps that the Government proposes 
to take in this direction to stop this public hazard and destruction of 
the quality of the water which will become a rare commodity in course 
of time. 
254 

[20 December, 2000]  RAJYA SABHA

Government* Peace Initiative in Jammu and Kashmir 
THE PRIME MINISTER (SHRI ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE): Sir, before 
the Winter Session of the Parliament concludes, and the House rises 
for the festival of Id and Christmas, I wish to take this opportunity and 
share with all hon. Members, the Government's assessment of the 
situation in Jammu and Kashmir, also along the LoC. 
Following my announcement of 19th November, that during 
the holy month of Ramzan, our security forces would not initiate 
operations against the militants, also expressing a hope that along 
the LoC too, infiltration would cease, there, have been some 
encouraging developments. Certain other aspects, however, remain 
as our continuing concerns. 
The Government is greatly heartened by the response of the 
citizens, political parties and other organisations in the State of 
Jammu and Kashmir. Our peace initiative has been widely welcomed 
there. A distinctly different and a more optimistic mood now prevails in 
that State. The constituency for peace has expanded significantly. 
There has also been a decline in incidents of terrorist 
violence in that State. Activities, however, of organisations like 
Lashkar-e-Tayaaba and Harkat-ul-Mujahedin continue, resulting in 
most unfortunate and regrettable loss of innocent civilian lives, also of 
the personnel of our security forces. The Government remains firm In 
its resolve to combating these and other challenges, also to defeating

SHRI R. MARGABANDU .(Tamil Nadu): Madam, I am not 
prepared to suppor t this Bill, unless an a ssurance is given by the 
Government that there will be a proper management of the banking 
system. Otherwise, there is no use of passing this Bill and increasing 
the authorised capital from Rs. 500 crores to Rs. 5,000 crores. When 
the employees in the banks are eating away the money in the 
banking sector. The purpose of this Bill is for the promotion and 
development of agriculture, small-scale and cottage and village 
industries, for rural development, securing prosperity for the rural

are three categories of persons who are approaching the banks for 
loan; first is the agriculturist, the other is the big landlord; and the third

agriculturists, nearly 80-90 per cent are small farmers, but that benefit 
does not go to them. When they approach the bank, loan is not given 
to them. If at all any loan is given, they will have to pay 10 per cent or

prepared to pay that. After availing of the loan, they do not repay it.

you say that it is for the benefit of the agriculturists? How do you say

areas? The sorry state of affairs is continuing. I quote one instance.

not repaying - the loan amount on account of failure

The second thing is with reference to clause 41 which deals 
with the right to adopt. Yesterday, I had pointed out, and I would like 
to reiterate, that the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 has 
a provision in se ction 11. I will pass on a co py to you, Madam, for 
your reference.   It states: 
"In every adoption the following conditions must be complied 
with: 
(1) "If the adoption is of a son, the adoptive father or 
mother, by whom the adoption is made, must not 
have a Hindu son, son's son or son's son's son, 
whether by legitimate blood relationship or by 
adoption, living at the time of adoption." 
This means that if you have son, you are not entitled to adopt 
a son. Similarly, there is a provision in the second clause about a 
daughter. If one has a daughter, he or she is not entitled to adopt a 
daughter. "This provision applies to Hindus, Jains, Buddhists and 
Sikhs" This is available at the top portion of the same page. 
"This Act applies - (a) to any person, who is a Hindu by 
religion in any of its forms or developments, including a Virashaiva, a 
Lingayat or a follower of the Brahmo, Prathana or Arya Samaj; (b) to 
any person who is a Buddhist, Jain or Sikh by religion, and (c) to any 
other person who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion." 
Therefore, this Personal Law appiicabie to the Hindus does not 
permit an adoption by a person if he already has a natural or an 
adopted son. Section 41 (2) of the present legislation also deals with 
adoption. Therefore, there is an enabling provision for adoption. The 
question that arises for consideration is this. There is no restriction 
here, as in the terms of the Adoption Act which has a prohibiting 
clause. There is no such clause here. You can adopt 10 or 15 or even 
20 children at a time. There is no problem that way. So, even If one 
has a natural son, he is free to adopt a boy. The protection that is 
available to a Hindu and others, who are already covered by the 
same provision, does not authorise an adoption, while the present 
statute seeks to allow adoption. I have two aspects to place for the 
consideration of the House. One is that, the bar that is there in this 
Act, applicable to Hindus, is being taken away, and an enabling 
provision with a contrary scope is being introduced by the proposed 
legislation. The second one is that there is a social element which 
one has to consider. When this 1956 Act was adopted, it was felt that 
the real purpose of the restrictive provision was on

account of the fact that if there is already a son or an adopted son, to 
adopt another stranger would create disharmony in the family and it 
would not have the family unit in proper shape. We are passing 
through difficult times. Social order and disctpline that used to be 
maintained earlier is absent. Social disorder has been spreading, and 
the family which is the basic natural unit, - this is recognised 
everywhere; even the Universal Declaration of Human Rights accept 
the family as a natural element or the first institution -- would get 
affected on account of the fact that the combination is not 
harmonious. If you import another boy from outside, when there is 
already a natural son or an adopted son, then there is bound to be 
dispute; there is bound to be chaos and disharmony. Therefore, the 
real legislative purpose behind the restriction introduced in the Hindu 
Adoption and v Maintenance Act, 1956, was for the purpose that the 
homogenity in the family may not be disrupted by introducing an alien 
element into the family. And that, if you already have a son, then there 
is no point in introducing another or in duplicating that. If that is taken 
into consideration, then, it will be easy to understand why such a 
restrictive provision is beneficial. I personally feel that many of you 
might have had the occasion to see families gett ing disrupted on 
account of almost a similar situation. In the Courts, as a lawyer and 
judge, I have handled many such cases where families have been 
disrupted on account of the fact that a stranger has been introduced, 
and homogenity has not been developed between the natural son and 
the adopted son. We have cases where, for example, after marriage, 
a child is not born. And thinking that the couple is growing and 
becoming old, they think of adoption. Soon after adoption, a natural 
son is born and brought into the family. Between the natural son, who 
is born later, and the son who has been adopted already, there used 
to be series of disputes. Earlier, it used to be that half of the share 
used to be given to the adopted son. After a natural son was born, the 
natural son would get double the share of the adopted son. But this is 
no more available tnat way and the system has, therefore, got to be 
rationalised. If this be the consideration, that the family must be 
saved, disruption should not come and homogenity should be 
maintained, one appreciates the baa,•_ the restriction; and if that was 
there, that should not be taken away.

OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shrimati Bedavati Buragohain and Shri Syed Abdul Malik, 
former Members of this House. 
Shrimati Bedavati passed away on 16th December, 2000, at the age of 79. 
Bom in North Lakhimpur, Assam, November, 1911, Shrimati Buragohain had 
her education at Dibrugarh and Bethune College, Calcutta, She was 
Headmistress, Government Girls M.C. School, Jorhat and was President of 
Tara Rama Dhyani L.P. School in 1952-53. She was a Member of the 
Central Social Welfare Board from 1954 to 1959. She was also associated 
with various social welfare organisations. Shrimati Bedavati Buragohain 
represented the State of Assam in this House from April, 1954 to April, 1960 
and again from April, 1960 to April, 1966. In the passing away of Shrimati 
Bedavati Buragohain, the country has lost a noted teacher and social worker. 
Shri Syed Abdul Malik passed away on  20th December, 2000, at the age 
of 81. Born at Naharani Village, Sibsagar, Assam January 1919. Shri Malik 
had his education at Cotton College, Guwahati. A teacher by profession, Shri 
Malik founded the Kuralguri High School in 1950 and served as its 
Headmaster during 1950-51. He was Professor of Assamese language and 
literature from 1951 to 1976 and also served as Head of the Department of 
Assamese, J.B. College, Jorhat. He was also a noted director actor and writer 
of screenplays for the cinema. Shri Malik had also several publications to his 
credit and represented India at the Asian Writers Conference in 1956-57. 
Shri Malik was also Editor of Assamese Encyclopedia, and literary magazines 
Taigam' and 'Zam Zam'. He received several cultural and literary awards, 
including the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1972. He was conferred the 
Padmashree in 1984 and Padmabhushan in 1992. Shri Syed Abdul Malik 
represented the State of Assam in this House from April, 1976 to April, 1982. 
In the passing away of Shri Syed 
1 

RAJYA SABHA (21 December, 2000] 
Abdul Malik, the country has lost a noted litterateur, an eminent linguist and 
a dedicated social worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shrimati Bedavati Buragohain and 
Shri Syed Abdul Malik. I request the Members to rise in their places and 
observe silence as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed.

*461. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Annual Plan  of many states including Orissa 
State has been drastically reduced; 
(b) whether it is because the State due to its financial constraints could not 
mobilise the resources; and 
(c) if so, whether Government are planning for any remedial measures to 
support to this category of financial weak States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PLANNING, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DE PARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE

Statement 
(a) No, Sir. States* (including Orissa) Plan outlays for the current year 2000-01 
have been finalized in consultation with the States concerned taking into 
consideration (i) the trend of aggregate actual resource mobilisation for the Plan 
of the State over the firs t three years of the Ninth Plan; and (ii) a realistic 
estimate of resources available for financing the Plan. Since most of the States 
had already budgeted relatively higher Plan size prior to holding of Annual Plan 
discussions, the more realistic Plan size based on identifiable resources that 
was finally agreed upon in accordance with the criteria indicated above has been 
termed the "Core Plan". During State Plan discussions that States were 
encouraged to mobilize additional resources to achieve a Plan size higher than 
the Core Plan size. At the same time, Core Plan outlays for 2000*01 are 
higher than previous year's revised approved Plan outlays in respect of all the 
States except Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Manipur and Punjab. A statement 
giving State-wise details of revised approved outlay for 1999-2000 and approved 
core Plan outlay for 2000-01 is at statement-I (See below). 
(b) The Mid Term Appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan revealed that as 
compared to the originally approved ou tlays, there were shortfalls in the 
resources mobilized by the States (including Orissa) during the first three years of 
the Ninth Five Year Plan. This was mainly because there had been a deterioration 
in the contribution of their own funds of the States to finance Plans, leading to 
increased dependence on borrowings to finance their Plan. The shortfall in the 
contribution of own funds of the States had in turn been mainly due to a 
deterioration in States' Balance from Current Revenue (BCR) and 
unsatisfactory performance of State Level Enterprises. A statement indicating 
the shares of central assistance, State's own funds and borrowings in the 
financing of the State Plan Outlay for Orissa is attached as statement-II (See 
below). 
(c) Planning Commission have been impressing upon the States to generate 
higher level of own resources inter-alia by improving the performance of State Level 
Enterprises, increasing tax and non-tax revenue and also by curtailing their non-
plan expenditure so that 
3

sufficient funds are available to finance the plan. In addition, joint efforts by the 
Centre and the states were initiated during 1999-2000 to evolve a strategy to 
address the fiscal issues confronting the financially weaker States in the 
form of a package of financial assistance to be provided by the centre alongwith 
an appropriate time bound programme of medium term fiscal reforms to be 
undertaken by the States. Thirteen States including Orissa have so far entered 
into an agreement (Memorandum of Understanding) with the Centre with a view to 
implement the fiscal reforms aiming at progressively improving the finances of 
the States. List of States which have entered into MoUs for fiscal reform is 
attached as statement-Ill. (See below). The Centre has made available financial 
assistance of Rs. 4490 crores so far to help these States tide over short-term 
difficulties and undertake fiscal reforms. Out of this, Rs. 300 crores has been 
released to Orissa.

Statement 
(a) and (b) The wholesale prices of certain agricultural commodities at some 
selected centres are ruling below the Minimum Support Price (MSP) announced

availability of certain agricultural commodities in our country and the declining 
trend in international prices of certain agricultural commodities. The cost of

increase in the prices of inputs such as diesel, fertilizers etc.

season and organizes purchase operations through public and cooperative agencies 
viz. Food Corporation of India (FO) for paddy, wheat and coarse cereals. Cotton 
Corporation of India (CCI) for cotton, Jute Corporation of India (JCI) for jute,

commodities, which are perishable in nature and which are grown mainly locally 
or where the cost differentia! varies substantially from State to State are covered 
under Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) of the Government. Large quantities 
of cereals etc. have been procured under the MSP scheme and procurement of 
certain commodities is continuing.

the country, the tariff levels have been bound for primary agricultural products 
and edible oils, with a few exceptions at 100 per cent, ISO per cent and 300 per 
cent respectively. The Government has been using instruments of trade to 
discourage the imports and encourage exports wherever necessary, and protect the

Marketing of agricultural products 
†*464. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': WiU the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage share of Government agencies in marketing of 
agricultural products; 
(b) whether there is a need to increase this share; 
(c) if so, how much and by when; and 
(d) the steps being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) to (d) The Food 
Corporation of India and State Governments/its Agencies mainly procure 
wheat and rice under price support operations. During the last few years, 
around 12 percent to 20 percent of the entire production of wheat and rice has 
been procured by them. Besides, the National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing 
Federation of India Limited (NAFED), which is the apex institution of 
marketing cooperatives in the country, is also engaged in marketing of 
agricultural commodities by implementing the Price Support Scheme for 
oilseeds, including copra, and pulses and the Market Intervention Scheme for 
horticultural and agricultural commodities which are perishable in nature. 
The extent of procurement and sales of agricultural produce by 
Government/its Agencies would depend upon the price situation prevailing in 
the country. Therefore, it is not feasible to indicate any percentage share for the 
Government agencies in respect of .procurement and sales of agricultural 
produce and products. In view of this, not time limit in this regard can be 
indicated.

Grievances of cyclone victims 
*465. SHRI GANDHI AZAD: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the victim s of cyclone expressed their agony 
and grievances against the Government of Orissa in a public hearing 
organised by the N.G.O.—"Centre for legal aid to poor" as reported in the 
New Indian Express, Bhubneshwar, dated 18th September, 2000; 
(b) whether large scale irregularities and injustice have been done to the 
cyclone victims; and 
(c) what corrective measures are being adopted in regard thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to 
(c) It is primarily the responsibility of the State Government to undertake 
necessary measures in the wake of natural calamities. The Government of 
India supplements the efforts of the St ate Government and has released the 
Central share of Calamity Relief Fund for 1999-2000 amounting to Rs. 42.50 
crore to the State Government for und ertaking necessary measures. Earlier 
Rs. 828.15 crores were released to the State, from the National Fund for 
Calamity Relief (NFCR) in the wake of floods and 2 cyclones, including the 
Super cyclone of October, 1999. Distribution of relief and undertaking relief 
measures at the ground level is the responsibility of the State Government. 
The Government of Orissa has informed that the Committee for Legal Aid 
to Poor (CLAP), a non-governmental organisation, had organised a public 
hearing on Orissa cyclone on 16th—17th September, 2000. The State 
Government is, however, reportedly not aware whether the cyclone victims 
have expressed their agony at the hearing organised by the CLAP. 
According to the State Government, there is no report of large scale 
irregularities and injustice to the cyclone victims and that the State 
Government have taken corrective meas ures wherever necessary. According 
to them house building assistance and ex-gratia payment in death cases has 
been paid in eligible cases. Senior Officers of the State Government in-
charge of the cyclone affected

Pakistan's Nuclear Programme 
*466. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that China has stepped up its aid to Pakistan's 
Nuclear Programme and Chinese experts were recently sighted around 
Pakistan's missile factory; 
(b) whether the US Government is aware of this and is sending a high level 
delegation to China to discuss the development; and 
(c) if so, Government's views in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) 
Government has noted reports to this effect. However, China continues to deny 
that it has provided any assistance to Pakistan's nuclear weapons or missile 
development programmes; it maintains that its relations with Pakistan are neither 
directed at nor are they at the expense of any third country. 
(b) Government has information of official US contacts with China armed at 
preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles. 
(c) These revelations are not new to us; they confirm the Government's 
own assessments. Government has consistently highlighted, including in 
bilateral discussions with the US and the People's Republic of China, the 
adverse effect on India's security from continuing nuclear and missile 
proliferation in Pakistan despite the existence of various export control regimes and 
declarations of restraint by supplier countries.

3463. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that America, Brazil, Mexico maintain herds of 
Brahman, Krishna, Cows/Bulls which are imported there from India; 
(b) whether the American Brahman breeders Association in Taxas encourages 
pure breeds of Bharatiya Cows/Bulls; 
(c) whether our native breeds are becoming extinct and/or used for exotic 
breeding with foreign blood, thereby loosing their characteristics of Drought 
Power; and 
(d) whether cross breed male calves are not found usable in 
agriculture or transportation and reach slaughter houses in young 
age? 
THE    MINISTER    OF    STATE    IN    THE    MINISTRY    OF 
AGRICULTURE   (DR.   DEBENDRA   PRADHAN);   (a)   and   (b) Yes, 
Sir. 
(c) and (d) Extinction of breeds because of rapid changes in the socio-economic 
and agroclimatic conditions across the world is a global phenomenon. Since it 
is not possible to meet the rising demand for milk of the fast growing human 
population in the country by exclusively following selective breeding of 
indigenous cattle breeds, it is necessary to infuse exotic germ-plasm in a part of the 
low producing non-descript indigenous cattle through crossbreeding. The 
population of indigenous cattle for outnumber the crossbred stock and the 
policy of the Government has been to insist on having a balanced 
improvement of cattle, both for milk and draught. Crossbred males are suitable 
for agriculture and transportation where the work-surface is not too muddy and 
when they are put to work during cooler hours of the day. Legislation exists in 
most of the states prohibiting slaughter of male calves at an early age.

3473. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has a geographical area of 329 hectares of which about 
23 per cent is barren and uncultivable land, cultivable wasteland, permanent 
pastures and fallow land; 
(b) whether it is a fact that per capita availability of land declined from 
0.89 hectares in the early 1950s to  0.37 hectares in mid 1990s and is 
expected to reduce further to 0.19 hectares by 
2000; 
(c) if the answers to both part above ar e in affirmative, what steps have 
been/are being taken to make land more cultivable; 
(d) which areas of land has been made usable till date; and

farmers and private farmers in the country? 
THE   MINISTER    OF    STATE   IN   THE   MINISTRY   OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) Geographical area 
of India is 329 million hectares of which about 23 per cent land is barren and 
unculturable land, culturable wastes 
75 

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2000] 
land,   permanent  pastures  and  other  grazing  lands,  land  under 
miscellaneous free crops and groves and fallow lands.

taken to make land more cultivable. It has since been decided

Governments. About 50 percent of the Geographical area

Programme (DDP) and Externally Aided Projects.

land holdings is 106.64 million, which includes 20.10 million small holdings 
and 63.4 million marginal holdings.

STATEMENT 
Joint Statement on the Visit to India by Gen. Maung Aye, Vice Chairman 
State Peace A Development Council, Myanmar 
1. H.E. General Maung Aye, Vice Chairman, State Peace & Development 
Council (SPDC), Deputy Commander-in-Chief, Myanmar Defence Forces and 
Commander-in-Chief, Myanmar Army paid a seven day visit to India from 14 to 
21 November, 2000 at the invitation of H.E. Shri Krishan Kant, Vice 
President of India. General Maung Aye was accompanied by a high-level 
delegation consisting of H.E. Lt. Gen. Tin Oo, Secretary-2, SPDC, H.E. Lt. 
Gen. Tin Hla, Deputy Prime Miister and Minister for Military 
131 

RAJYA SABHA (21 December, 2000] 
Affairs, H.E. Maj. Gen. Soe Win, Member of the SPDC and Commander of 
the North-West Command, H.E. U Win Aung, Minister for Foreign Affairs, 
H.E. U Aung Thaung, Minister for Indus try-1, H.E. U Khin Maung Thein, 
Minister for Finance and Revenue, H.E. U Thaung, Minister for Science and 
Technology, H.E. Maj. Gen. Tin Htut, Minister for Electric Power, H.E. 
Brig. Gen. Pyi Sone, Minister for Commerce and H.E. U Khin Maung Kyaw, 
Dy. Minister of Industry-II, and other senior officials. 
2. During this visit, the leaders of the two countries held discussions on 
bilateral, regional and international issues. They discussed measures to create 
favourable conditions for the rapid development of bilateral relations. 
3. Relations between India and Myanmar are civilizational in nature and 
rooted in a common cultural and religious heritage and geographical 
contiguity. Leaders of both countries have always maintained a tradition of 
high level exchanges and personal rapport. With the visit by General Maung 
Aye this process has been enhanced. 
4. In Delhi, H.E. General Maung Aye and Daw Mya Mya San were 
accorded a warm ceremonial welcome by H.E. Shri Krishan Kant, Vice 
President of India and Shrimati Suman Krishan Kant. H.E, General Maung 
Aye and Daw Mya Mya San called on H.E.  Shri K.R. Narayanan, President 
of India and Shrimati Usha Narayanan. He held discussions with H.E. the 
Vice President, H.E. Shri Atal Bihari  Vajpayee, Prime Mi nister, H.E. Shri 
Jaswant Singh, Minister of External Affairs, H.E. Shri L.K. Advani, Home 
Minister, Shri Omar Farooq Abdulla, Minister of State for Commerce & 
Industry, and Shrimati Sonia Gandhi, Leader of Opposition. 
5. The discussions between the Prime Minister and the Vice Chairman, 
State Peace & Development Council covered a wide range of areas, including 
economic cooperation, trade, cro ss border projects and activities, 
international, terrorism, drug trafficking, cooperation in the field of culture, 
human resource development, science and technology, and regional 
cooperation within the framework of BIMST-EC, of which both countries 
are members, as also under the 
132 

[21  December, 2000] RA*r"A SABHA 
aegis of India-ASEAN dialogue partnership. The two sides expressed 
satisfaction at the ail round progress in relations in the past few years. At the 
same time, it was agreed that the present level of interaction, specially in the 
economic and commercial fields did not reflect the potential of such 
relations. Both sides reaffirmed their desire to promote bilateral relations to a 
qualitatively higher and dynamic stage. They also agreed that they could 
benefit from various regional cooperation programmes in which they are 
participating, such as BIMST-EC and India-ASEAN cooperation. 
6. -The two sides agreed to take st eps to ensure peace" and tranquillity 
along the India-Myanmar border, and to give content to cross border 
cooperation, which would directly benefit populations living on both sides of 
the border. They recognized the need to establish the necessary infrastructure 
in terms of cross border transport and communication links, promote more 
frequent exchanges both at the government and people-to-people level, and 
actively encourage the business communities of both countries to take 
advantage of the many economic complementarities between the two 
countries. The Tamu-Kalemyo highway which will link India's northeast with 
the western part of the Myanmar and beyond would contribute singnificantly 
to this cross border cooper ation. The highway is expected to be handed over 
soon to the Myanmar Government. 
7. The two sides also discussed progress in other proposed cross border 
projects, viz. the Tamanthi Hydroelectric project and the Kaladan River 
Navigation, Road and Gas Pipeline Project, and agreed to take necessary 
steps to expedite ongoing investigations and feasibility studies. 
8. An agreement to extend a US$ 15 million India credit to Myanmar was 
signed during the visit by the Finance Ministers of the two countries. Both 
sides noted with satisfaction that an earlier Indian credit of US$ 10 million 
was utilized by the Myanmar side for setting up industrial plants and for 
supply of railway rolling stock. The new credit line will also be used for 
sourcing industrial and electrical equipment from India. 
9. During his stay in India H.E. General Maung Aye and his

delegation visited places of Buddhist pilgrimage. General Maung Aye also 
travelled to Bangalore where he visited a number of scientific and industrial 
establishments and organisations working in the fields of Information Technology, 
industrial and agricultural machinery, electronics, agriculture, aeronautics and space 
research. In Delhi, the Confederation of Indian Industry hosted a lunche on in 
honour of General Maung Aye and his delegation to enable them to meet and 
interact with leading Indian businessmen and industrialists and discuss possibilities 
of cooperation. General Maung Aye and his delegation also visited Agra and 
Udaipur. 
10. H.E. General Maung Aye extended a cordial invitation to H.E. Shri 
Krishaa Kant, Vice President of India to pay an official visit to Myanmar. The 
invitation was accepted with pleasure. Mu tually convenient dates for the visit 
will be decided through diplomatic channels.

extended cordial invitations to H.E. Shri K.R. Narayanan, President of India and 
Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee, Prime Minister of India, respectively to pay visits to 
Myanmar. The invitations were accep ted with pleasur e and mutually 
convenient dates would be decided through diplomatic channels. The President 
and Prime Minister of India respectively requested H.E. General Maung Aye to 
convey to H.E. Senior General Than Shwe an invitation to visit India at a 
mutually convenient date.

die warm and friendly reception and gracious hospitality extended to the 
delegation.

(b) and (c) Making the administration corruption free, accountable,

corruption at all levels. In the Ministries/Departments etc of the Central 
Government, the Secretary and the Head of the Department concerned is 
responsible for ensuring probity and integrity in their respective organisations. 
A three pronged strategy of Surveillance, Prevention and Punitive/ Deterrent 
action is followed by the Government in this regard. Recognising that an 
important aspect of Preventive Vigilance is to ensure transparency in public 
administration, measures of administrative reforms such as introduction of 
Citizens' Charters and setting up of Facilitation Centres have been initiated. The 
review and simplification of laws, rules and procedures has also been taken 
up. The punitive actions being taken under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 
1988 duly supported by various rules governing the service conditions of 
public servants, also act as a deterrent  against corruption. An anti-corruption 
unit is functioning in the Prime Mini ster's Office since 1997 to monitor 
complaints of corruption received in that Office.

Commission has also recognized that one of the main factors which hinder plan 
implementation is governance which, infer^alia, include corruption. Planning

be established for successful execution of the Plan and further private

recent past towards eradication of  corruption from public services, inter-alia 
include introduction of Central Vigilance Commission Bill on 20.12.1999 in 
the Lok Sabha. Apart from this, the Freedom of Information Bill, 2000 has 
also been introduced in the Lok Sabha on 25.7.2000 to bring greater 
transparency and accountability in the functioning of the Government.

August, 1998 and lapsed on the dissolution of the House on 26.4.1999. The

environment.

Seventy Fourth Constitutional Amendment Acts bestowed Cons titutional 
status to the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). Panchayati Raj Bodies which 
came into existence in the States pursuant to the Constitutional Amendments 
were delegated administrative and finanical powers in areas which are critical to 
the livelihoods of the population. The PRIs have also been given a greater say 
in execution and monitoring of developmental process. 
Major poverty alleviation programmes have been restructured to address the 
needs of the people in a more focused manner. Areas Development Programmes 
have been given a fillip. Basic services to the people have been sought to be 
provided under the Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). rural 
connectivity which enables people not only to increase their incomes but also 
diversify the livelihood options has been given a high priority under the PMGY. 
Social security provided through the National Social Assistance Programme 
(NSAP) has been widened and deepened. These changes are expected to enable 
the community at large to take advantage of the reform process and better their 
living conditions in the rural areas. 
Economic reform is a continuous process involving changes in a wide range 
of policies and procedures. The board direction of reforms has been outlined in 
the Ninth Five Year Plan and the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan 
documents. Further direction would be provided in the Tenth Five Year Plan, on 
which work has just commenced. Detailed reforms regarding each sector are being 
announced as and when required.

3592. SHRI SURESH KALMADI:  Will the Minister of ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a plan has been envisaged for the construction of 
National Highways from North to South and East to West in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps Government propose to take to implement this plan alongwith the 
likely expenditure to be incurred and the benefits that will be accrued from this 
plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS [MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI]: 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A plan called the National Highway Development 
Project (NHDP) consisting of Golden Quadrilateral connecting the four 
metropolitan cities of Delhi, Calcutta, Chennai, Mumbai and Delhi and North-
South corridor connecting Srinagar to Kanyakumari alongwith Salem-Cochin 
section at its spur; and East-West corridor connecting Stlchar to Porbandar has 
been envisaged for 4/6 Inning in a total length of 13,252 km. The total cost 
of the NHDP is estimated to be Rs. 54,000 crores. 
(c) National Highways Authority of India has been authorized to implement the 
Project. Government has approved the Project in principle and subsequently has 
approved a programme of 40 sub-projects in a length of 4,659 km during the two 
years, i.e. 2000-2001 and 2001-2002. The benefits envisaged from the project are 
removal of congestion, reduction of vehicle operating cost and savings in 
travel time, thereby providing an impetus to the overall economic devleopment.

AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN
